expected: This is an AI-narrated walkthrough of Research Loop, a repeatable intelligence pipeline for student researchers. The series asks which experimental tasks agents can automate, and what makes the results trustworthy. The display presents excerpts from retained project artifacts, rather than pretending to be a live collection. The main Bash entry point coordinates independent components for feeds, YouTube, podcasts, extraction, storage, editorial decisions, and drafting. Python implements each component. Only the storage interface accesses the SQLite evidence index. Articles and video scripts share an evidence-linked brief. A separate packaging command checks the reviewed fingerprint and a matching student decision. It does not fetch new sources or silently rewrite approved drafts.

expected: Here is a concrete claim from the first article. Li and Lu report contact precision increasing from twenty-eight point two percent to thirty-six point six percent at the same forty-eight point four billion token budget. The source passage also says a human decided which recipes to scale. The brief retains the exact item identifier, source version, and quotation. The article therefore attributes the numbers to the authors and preserves the human role. It does not describe an independently replicated result or a fully autonomous discovery. This chain matters because a fluent summary can otherwise erase the condition that makes a reported result interpretable. The saved article and its free published version can be compared directly.

Original-page recovery was labeled supplemental evidence, so it could not silently satisfy the RSS quota. On the second date, the native feeds succeeded and expanded the corpus. That distinction lets a reader separate a lack of coverage from a lack of new research. Publication dates are also separate from collection times. Old, unknown, and future dates are handled explicitly. Isolated contract tests exercise date boundaries, partial failure, source versions, and approval invalidation. Those tests use synthetic fixtures and are not counted as research evidence or live collection runs.

expected: The student compared three accepted and three rejected cases with the saved AI decisions. One accepted tutorial was restricted to procedural guidance: it cannot prove that a model is stronger. The student also requested human review of AI evaluations to reduce the risk of a model judging its own output. Another accepted paper must remain an author-reported result with its human role visible. Conflicting numbers must be disclosed rather than turned into a speed or cost superiority claim. News digests supply leads, not independent confirmation. These recorded judgments informed policy version three. The editorial rerun reused the frozen October fifteenth evidence, so it is not a third collection. The human-review safeguard appears in article three and its matching narration.

expected: All three articles are published free, and their three companion videos are unlisted on YouTube, with reciprocal links. Mechanical content checks pass. The student approved the finished videos after listening and explicitly authorized publication of the articles. This does not establish that every original audio quotation has been heard and checked. Those source excerpts remain on the final listening checklist. The main architectural tradeoff is additional artifacts and storage in exchange for inspectable evidence and reproducible decisions. Retaining source versions also makes stale approval detectable after a draft changes. Local transcription and speech generation avoid a per-call hosted audio fee, but consume machine resources. Codex subscription usage cannot be reliably converted into dollars here, so its cost remains unknown, not free.
